Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- Test setup and intent:
  - The test constructs two simple positional Arguments (“input” and “output”), each with minimum=1 and maximum=1, and combines them into a composite SourceDestArgument. The enclosing Group contains only this composite argument. It then parses four identical tokens: ["testfile.txt", "testfile.txt", "testfile.txt", "testfile.txt"] and expects an OptionException with the message "Unexpected testfile.txt while processing ".
  - The intended behavior here is that the composite argument can consume at most two values (one for source and one for destination). The remaining tokens should be reported as unexpected. The “LoopingOptionLookAlike” name indicates this is specifically exercising the parser’s loop-prevention logic when it repeatedly sees an argument that “looks like” something it can process but shouldn’t anymore.

- How parsing proceeds in code:
  - Parser.parse(String[]) creates a List of arguments with “fresh” String objects (new String(argument)) so that object identity (==) can be used to detect lack of progress in the loop (lines 61–67).
  - It constructs the WriteableCommandLine and crucially applies model defaults before parsing via group.defaults(commandLine) (line 73).
  - The main loop repeatedly checks group.canProcess(commandLine, iterator). If canProcess is true, it peeks the next token, remembers it in previous, and calls group.process(commandLine, iterator). If on a subsequent iteration the same object instance is encountered again (i.e., process didn’t advance the iterator), it breaks to avoid looping (lines 79–93).
  - If any tokens remain after the loop, Parser throws an OptionException with the UNEXPECTED_TOKEN message key and the unexpected token (lines 96–100). OptionException then formats the message and appends usage text of the Option that raised it (the group) (constructor shows it does helper.getMessage(...) + " " + option.appendUsage(...)).

- Composite argument behavior and why “looping look-alike” matters:
  - SourceDestArgument combines two child Arguments and sets its total min/max to the sum of the children (constructor lines 71–73). With both children having max=1, the composite max is 2.
  - SourceDestArgument.canProcess(commandLine, arg) currently returns true if either child argument can process the next token (source.canProcess(...) || dest.canProcess(...)). It does not incorporate the composite’s own max directly.
  - The test’s repeated identical tokens make the “canProcess/process” coordination critical: once both children have reached their maximum, process must stop consuming and the loop should then terminate and report the first remaining token as unexpected. The loop-prevention guard (previous == next) enforces this.

- Where the bug manifests (interaction with defaults):
  - Parser applies defaults before any user-supplied values (group.defaults(commandLine), line 73).
  - With defaults present, the command line can already hold values for arguments before parsing begins. This is exactly the “current bug report” scenario: defaults are treated as if the arguments are already set, so subsequent user-supplied values are rejected as “additional” rather than overriding the defaults.
  - In this configuration, child Arguments in SourceDestArgument see “already has a value” and refuse to consume user tokens. That means SourceDestArgument.process is unable to make progress on a token that still “looks” valid to canProcess, leading the parser’s loop-prevention to trigger and bail out to an OptionException.
  - The test expects a specific OptionException message for the first unconsumed “testfile.txt”. However, because defaults were counted as real values, the timing/point at which the parser fails no longer matches the expected flow. The message is constructed by OptionException for the Group and includes the helper-composed text and appended usage; with defaults interfering, what gets appended (or which token is flagged) can differ, causing the assertion to fail.

- Root cause and link to the bug report:
  - The root issue is that defaults are applied too early and are treated as authoritative values. This prevents user-supplied command-line values from being accepted to satisfy required arguments or to override defaults, and in composite/positional scenarios like SourceDestArgument it leads to “look-alike” non-progress and the wrong error being reported.
  - This matches the current bug report: “argument defaults prevent commandline usage.” Applying defaults up front makes the parser think the arguments already have values, blocking intended overrides and breaking the expected parse/validation path demonstrated by this test.

In short: Parser.parse preloads defaults into the CommandLine before parsing. For composite positional arguments (SourceDestArgument), this causes the child arguments to refuse real input as “additional” rather than overriding defaults. The parser’s loop-prevention then kicks in, but the failure point/message no longer matches the test’s expectation, leading to the test failure.
